naive_rag.query: Compare the probe early-warning range in Section 4.2 with the false alarm trade-offs in Section 4.4 in Pre-Crime for Agents.
naive_rag.response_text:
The probe's early-warning capability and the trade-offs relating to false alarms are crucial components of the study "Pre-Crime for Agents." In Section 4.2 (not provided here), the probe's early-warning range likely deals with its ability to detect potential leaks or unauthorized actions before they occur, positioning itself as a preventative measure. While specific details from Section 4.2 are not directly provided in the documents, Section 6 of the discussion notes that the probe is best interpreted as a detector of a coming disclosure, particularly flagging when the value has just been read or when pressured into disclosure (Section 6).

In Section 4.4, the study delves into the trade-offs associated with false alarms of the probe. The cost of flags (essentially false alarms) is dependent on the action taken upon a flag. If each flag leads to a review, the per-call rate determines the workload. However, if a flag stops the whole agent, the focus shifts to whether an episode sees at least one flag. This section highlights that 59% of episodes saw at least one flag when operating at a nominal 5% rate because flags cluster in the same episodes (Section 4.4).

A stricter threshold is discussed for halting an agent, accounting for cluster behavior of flags, and is set per episode rather than per call. Such a per-episode threshold demonstrates that about one in twenty refusing episodes sees a flag (Section 4.4). More importantly, it catches 26% of leaking episodes by their first leak and 21% of leaking calls, with a minimal flagging rate of 0.1% of calls in refusing episodes.

Pairing the probe with a cheap text check did not yield noticeable gains; in fact, strict thresholds where both have to agree might discard leaks the probe could catch alone. This pairing approach was further discussed with no significant advantage observed, missing many leaks due to the stricter requirement for concurrence (Section 4.4).

In summary, the early-warning range of the probe is quite effective close to an event, especially just after data is accessed under pressure, while the false alarm trade-offs illustrate a balance between early detection and operational cost, with the latter being manageable through structured thresholds and action plans. The probe scores are generally insensitive to rule text changes, catching disclosures even when allowed, by closely monitoring call dynamics (Section 6).
